case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress authorized cumulative punishments (and thus the Double Jeopardy Clause allows separate convictions/sentences) for the same firearm-related conduct under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) (using/carrying/possessing a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence or drug trafficking crime) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (causing death with a firearm in the course of violating § 924(c)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both charges arise from the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so the Blockburger/Double Jeopardy presumption against multiple punishments applies unless Congress clearly indicated otherwise. He contends there is no such clear authorization: Congress expressly provided cumulative-punishment language in certain parts of § 924(c) (e.g., for some predicates/recidivist situations) but did not include comparable language authorizing stacking § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same conduct. Therefore, entering and cumulatively sentencing on both convictions violates the Double Jeopardy Clause (or, framed as statutory interpretation to avoid a double-jeopardy problem), requiring vacatur of one conviction/sentence and resentencing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States, in an unusual posture, supports Barrett on the merits in the Supreme Court: it agrees § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), that this triggers a presumption against cumulative punishments, and that Congress did not clearly rebut that presumption with an affirmative indication that it intended § 924(c) and § 924(j) to be stacked for the same conduct. The government emphasizes statutory text and structure: § 924(c) sometimes expressly authorizes cumulative punishment, but it does not do so for the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing; thus cumulative sentences are not authorized. The court-appointed amicus (supporting the judgment below) counters that cumulative punishments are permissible because the statutes address different harms/penalties and that Congress’s intent to add punishment for firearm use and for death-causing firearm use can be inferred without requiring duplicative cumulative-punishment language in both provisions (invoking Missouri v. Hunter-style reasoning).
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi (Alito, J., dissenting, on GVR practice)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that Congress designed § 924(j) as an aggravated add-on to § 924(c), implicitly authorizing cumulative punishment—runs into the Blockburger reality that § 924(j)’s “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” incorporates every element of § 924(c) and adds death, making (c) a lesser-included offense. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Whalen/Rutledge therefore require a clear indication of cumulative intent, and I agree with Justice Barrett’s structural point that Congress speaks unmistakably when it wants stacking (e.g., § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)), yet it said nothing comparable for a (c)/(j) pairing. Lora’s recognition that § 924(j) sits outside § 924(c)’s sentencing regime further cautions against importing § 924(c)’s add-on logic by implication. A minimalist holding—limited to same firearm use and same predicate offense—resolves the double-jeopardy multiple-punishments problem without opining on other charging permutations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that Congress’s evident desire to increase punishment for firearm violence implies § 924(j) was meant to stack atop § 924(c), especially given § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentence command. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, our task is textual: § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which incorporates all (c) elements and adds death, making (c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger and triggering Whalen/Rutledge’s presumption against cumulative punishment absent a clear statement. Missouri v. Hunter makes legislative intent dispositive, yet—consistent with Justice Kagan’s structural point—Congress elsewhere used explicit “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language when it wanted stacking, and § 924(j) contains no comparable authorization to impose both punishments for the same unit of conduct. Lora’s separation of § 924(j) from § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery further undercuts importing (c)’s add-on logic by implication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense meant to stack with § 924(c)’s generally cumulative regime—still founders on the enacted text: § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress) makes (c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggers Blockburger’s presumption against multiple punishments. Under Missouri v. Hunter/Whalen/Rutledge, that presumption is overcome only by a clear statement of cumulative intent, and Justice Barrett’s point is decisive for me: Congress expressly mandated consecutive/cumulative punishment in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) but did not do so for a (c)/(j) pairing, so we should not infer stacking by implication. Lora’s recognition that § 924(j) sits outside § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery further supports treating (j) as an aggravated alternative penalty for the same conduct rather than an automatic add-on. I therefore would vacate one conviction/sentence when both counts are based on the same firearm use and predicate offense.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 924(j) is a freestanding homicide offense and Congress implicitly expected an additional § 924(c) conviction because § 924(c) usually stacks—still runs into the multiple-punishments rule: under Blockburger, § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense when (j) requires death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so Whalen/Rutledge demand a clear statement to cumulate. Justice Kagan’s elements-focused point is decisive for me: incorporation of all (c) elements plus death is not the kind of separation that defeats the same-offense presumption. Justice Barrett’s structural observation—that Congress knew how to require “in addition to” and consecutive punishment in § 924(c) but did not do so for a (c)/(j) pairing—underscores that we should not infer authorization to multiply punishment from silence, particularly after Lora’s insistence that § 924(j) has its own sentencing architecture. Given the grave real-world consequences of unauthorized stacking and the rule of lenity’s pull in penal ambiguity, I would vacate one conviction/sentence and remand for resentencing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best move—invoking Missouri v. Hunter/Garrett to say Congress implicitly authorized cumulative punishment because § 924(j) cross-references § 924(c)—still runs into the text: as the Chief Justice Roberts stresses, § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which necessarily incorporates every (c) element and makes (c) lesser-included under Blockburger on the same firearm use/predicate. Under Whalen/Rutledge, that triggers a presumption against multiple punishments that Hunter allows Congress to override only with clear indicia of cumulation; Justice Barrett’s point about Congress’s unmistakable “in addition to”/consecutive drafting elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores how conspicuous the silence is here. Lora’s separation of § 924(j) from § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery reinforces that we should not import (c)’s add-on architecture by implication, so the better, workable reading is to vacate one duplicative conviction/sentence when both counts rest on the same unit of conduct.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(j)’s separate codification and distinct penalties suggest Congress intended it as an additional tool that may be stacked with § 924(c). But as the Chief Justice notes, § 924(j) is triggered only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which textually incorporates every § 924(c) element and adds one more, making (c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger and invoking Whalen/Rutledge’s presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear contrary statement. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is decisive for me: Congress expressly mandates consecutive, cumulative punishment when it wants it, so we should not infer stacking authorization from mere placement or silence. Lora further cautions against importing § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery into § 924(j) by implication, reinforcing that the better reading is (j) as the aggravated alternative penalty for death-causing conduct, not a mandatory add-on to a separate (c) sentence for the same act.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 924(j) is codified outside § 924(c) with its own penalties and thus signals a separate, cumulatively punishable offense—doesn’t overcome Blockburger, which turns on statutory elements rather than codification. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggering Whalen/Rutledge’s presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear statement. Justice Barrett’s structural observation is decisive for me institutionally: Congress expressly mandated consecutive/cumulative punishment elsewhere in § 924(c), so the absence of comparable language for a (c)/(j) pairing is meaningful under Missouri v. Hunter. Lora’s recognition that § 924(j) has a distinct sentencing scheme further counsels against importing § 924(c)’s stacking regime by implication, so the workable course is to vacate one conviction/sentence and remand.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(j) is a distinct offense and, given Congress’s evident desire to enhance gun-violence penalties, should be stackable with § 924(c). But as Chief Justice Roberts underscores, § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which textually incorporates all § 924(c) elements and adds death, making (c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggering Blockburger’s presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear contrary indication. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Congress’s demonstrated ability to mandate cumulation expressly—contrasted with the absence of any “in addition to” or comparable authorization for a (c)/(j) pairing—confirms that Missouri v. Hunter’s legislative-intent test is not satisfied by implication alone. Lora’s recognition that § 924(j) sits outside § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery further cautions against importing § 924(c)’s stacking logic into (j) without textual direction, so the duplicative conviction/sentence should be vacated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that § 924(j) looks like an aggravated, freestanding homicide provision that Congress likely expected to stack on top of § 924(c)’s consecutive regime to ensure extra punishment. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which necessarily incorporates every § 924(c) element and makes (c) a lesser-included offense on the same conduct—triggering Whalen/Rutledge’s presumption against cumulative punishment absent a clear statement. Justice Barrett’s observation that Congress elsewhere spoke explicitly when it wanted stacking (including § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive command) makes the absence of parallel “in addition to” language here meaningful, and Lora reinforces that we should not import § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery into § 924(j) by implication. Given the real-world stakes of unauthorized cumulation—gratuitous overpunishment in a system already prone to it—I would vacate one conviction/sentence and remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly applies only when a defendant, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” causes death, so a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation is a necessary component of § 924(j) on these facts, triggering the Blockburger presumption against cumulative punishments for the same conduct. Under Missouri v. Hunter and Albernaz, that presumption can be overcome only by a clear indication of congressional intent to authorize stacking, but Congress did not include an “in addition to” directive for a § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing comparable to the explicit cumulative-punishment language elsewhere in § 924(c). Read as a matter of statutory interpretation (and consistent with Lora’s treatment of § 924(j) as distinct from § 924(c)’s sentencing regime), the better construction is that Congress authorized punishment under § 924(j) for the death-causing firearm use but did not also authorize a separate, cumulative § 924(c) conviction and sentence for the same firearm use during the same predicate crime. Accordingly, one of the convictions/sentences must be vacated to avoid an unauthorized multiple-punishment outcome under the Double Jeopardy Clause.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling inquiry is statutory: whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishments for the same conduct under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j). Section 924(j) expressly applies only "in the course of a violation of subsection (c)," so a § 924(c) violation is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States, triggering the presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear contrary indication. Nothing in the text or structure of § 924(c) or § 924(j) contains the kind of affirmative authorization for stacking that Missouri v. Hunter permits when the legislature clearly intends cumulative punishment, and Congress’s inclusion of explicit cumulative-punishment directives elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores the absence of such authorization here. Because the Double Jeopardy Clause forbids imposing greater punishment than Congress has authorized, one of the duplicative convictions/sentences must be vacated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 924(j) by its own terms applies only when the defendant, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” causes death, which makes § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use and predicate crime. Under Blockburger v. United States, that triggers the presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear indication Congress authorized stacking, and the text and structure here cut the other way: Congress expressly specified cumulative and consecutive punishment rules in parts of § 924(c) (including § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)), yet included no comparable authorization for imposing separate convictions and sentences for § 924(c) and § 924(j) based on the same conduct. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments only where the legislature has made its intent clear, and inferring such intent here would disregard Congress’s selective use of explicit cumulative-punishment language and create unnecessary double-jeopardy tension. Vacating one conviction and resentencing still leaves ample room to impose severe punishment for a death-causing firearm use under § 924(j), without unauthorized stacking.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly applies only when the defendant causes death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States. That triggers the Double Jeopardy presumption against cumulative punishments unless Congress clearly indicated otherwise, and nothing in § 924(j) or the surrounding structure supplies the kind of clear authorization Missouri v. Hunter and Albernaz v. United States require to overcome that presumption—especially given that Congress knew how to speak clearly when it wanted stacking in § 924(c) itself. Reading the statutes to permit automatic stacking here would risk imposing greater punishment than Congress intended, contrary to the core Double Jeopardy principle governing multiple punishments in a single proceeding. The proper remedy is to vacate one conviction/sentence and remand for resentencing so punishment can be imposed under the provision Congress unmistakably authorized.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation is necessarily included within any § 924(j) conviction arising from the same firearm use and predicate crime, making the two counts the “same offense” under Blockburger. Under Whalen/Rutledge, cumulative convictions and sentences are barred absent a clear indication that Congress authorized stacking, and nothing in § 924(j)’s text or § 924(c)’s structure supplies that authorization for this pairing—especially given that Congress elsewhere in § 924(c) used explicit cumulative-punishment/consecutive-sentencing language. Missouri v. Hunter and Garrett confirm that Congress can authorize cumulative punishment, but they require a clear legislative signal gleaned from text/structure/history; here, the better reading is that § 924(j) provides an alternative, aggravated penalty for death-causing conduct “in the course of” a § 924(c) violation, not an additional mandatory add-on. Reading the statutes this way also yields a more workable, coherent scheme consistent with Lora’s emphasis on careful attention to the distinct sentencing architecture of § 924(j) versus § 924(c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes it a separate offense only by requiring that, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” the defendant cause death with a firearm; that text incorporates every element of § 924(c)(1)(A) and then adds the death element, making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger. Under Albernaz and Missouri v. Hunter, cumulative punishments are permissible only when Congress clearly authorizes them, but nothing in § 924(j) or the surrounding structure supplies that clear indication—especially given that § 924(c) elsewhere uses explicit consecutive/cumulative-punishment language, yet says nothing about stacking (c) with (j) for the same conduct. Lora reinforces reading these provisions as Congress wrote them, not as courts might wish them to operate at sentencing, and any lingering ambiguity about cumulative punishment must be resolved against multiplying penalties. The Double Jeopardy Clause therefore bars separate convictions/sentences for the same act under both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j) absent clearer congressional direction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of Section 924(j) when both charges rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so under Blockburger the default presumption is that Congress did not authorize cumulative punishments for the same conduct. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative punishments only when Congress gives a clear indication of that intent, and here the statutory text and structure cut the other way: Congress expressly provided cumulative-punishment directives in parts of Section 924(c), but did not include comparable authorization to stack a Section 924(c) conviction with a Section 924(j) conviction for the same act. Consistent with judicial restraint and practical workability, we should resolve the statutory ambiguity to avoid a Double Jeopardy problem and vacate one conviction/sentence and remand for resentencing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(j) applies only when a defendant, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” causes death with a firearm, so on its face it incorporates all the elements of § 924(c)(1)(A) plus the additional element of death—making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger v. United States. That triggers the presumption against cumulative punishments for the same conduct unless Congress has clearly indicated a contrary intent, and nothing in the text or structure of § 924(j) affirmatively authorizes stacking an additional § 924(c) conviction and sentence on top of § 924(j) for the same firearm use. By contrast, when Congress intends cumulative punishment within § 924(c), it knows how to say so expressly (e.g., § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentence command), reinforcing that the absence of comparable authorization for a § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing leaves the Blockburger presumption unrebutted. Under Garrett v. United States and Missouri v. Hunter, the question is legislative intent; here, the best reading of the enacted text is that Congress authorized punishment under § 924(j) for the death-causing firearm use, not cumulative punishment under both provisions for the same unit of conduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” making a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation a necessary component—and thus a lesser-included offense—of § 924(j) for the same conduct. Under Blockburger and Albernaz, that triggers a presumption against cumulative punishments unless Congress provides a sufficiently clear indication to the contrary, and nothing in the text or structure of § 924(c) or § 924(j) clearly authorizes stacking § 924(c) punishment “in addition to” § 924(j) for the same firearm use and predicate crime. Missouri v. Hunter allows multiple punishments only when the legislature clearly authorizes them, but here Congress used explicit “in addition to” language in § 924(c) with respect to the predicate crime—not with respect to § 924(j)—and the absence of comparable authorization counsels against cumulative convictions/sentences. Construing the statutes to avoid a Double Jeopardy multiple-punishment problem also best promotes procedural fairness and prevents gratuitous overpunishment where § 924(j) already captures the gravamen of the conduct (death caused with a firearm during the § 924(c) violation).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress authorized (and the Double Jeopardy Clause permits) cumulative convictions and sentences for the same conduct under 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (murder with a firearm in the course of a § 924(c) offense) and § 924(c)(1)(A) (using/carrying a firearm during and in relation to that same predicate crime).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) because § 924(j) incorporates § 924(c) as an element (a § 924(j) violation occurs only when the defendant causes death “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c)). Under Blockburger and the lesser-included-offense doctrine, that overlap triggers a presumption that Congress did not intend multiple punishments for the same act. Barrett contends nothing in the text or structure clearly rebuts that presumption: Congress expressly authorizes stacking in some § 924(c) contexts but did not expressly authorize cumulative punishment between § 924(c) and § 924(j). Therefore one of the two convictions (typically the lesser, § 924(c)) must be vacated to avoid unconstitutional multiple punishment for the same offense.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States, unusually, supports Barrett’s bottom-line: it agrees § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) and that the Double Jeopardy multiple-punishment analysis turns on congressional intent. The government argues the Blockburger presumption against multiple punishments has not been rebutted because there is no clear indication Congress meant to allow cumulative punishment for § 924(c) plus § 924(j) based on the same conduct. In particular, Congress knew how to authorize cumulative punishment explicitly within § 924(c) (for certain predicate offenses or circumstances) but did not do so for § 924(c) paired with § 924(j); that omission is best read as deliberate. The court-appointed amicus (supporting affirmance) counters that Congress’s intent to allow cumulative punishment can be inferred from § 924(c)’s general consecutive-sentencing regime and statutory design, relying on cases like Missouri v. Hunter to argue explicit cumulative-punishment language need not appear in both statutes; on that view, separate convictions and cumulative sentences are permissible.
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi (Alito, J., dissenting) (GVR standard)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a broad anti-lenity, pro-stacking policy, but that general directive is naturally read to govern how a sentence imposed “under this subsection” runs relative to the predicate offense—not to supply the clear statement Missouri v. Hunter requires to impose two punishments when § 924(c) is wholly subsumed within § 924(j) for the same act. Justice Kagan’s observation is persuasive that, after Lora confirms § 924(j) is not subject to § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive rule, it is even harder to treat § 924(c)’s sentencing provisions as an implied authorization for cumulative § 924(c)+§ 924(j) convictions. Justice Barrett’s point that Congress expressly addressed stacking elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores that silence as to this pairing is not the kind of unmistakable congressional instruction that overcomes Blockburger/Whalen’s presumption against multiple punishments. A narrow disposition—vacating the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving § 924(j) intact—respects precedent and avoids broader pronouncements about § 924(j) beyond this double-punishment context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language signals a broad pro-cumulative-punishment policy, but that language is naturally read—just as the Chief Justice explains—to ensure a § 924(c) sentence is consecutive to the underlying predicate offense, not to authorize a second punishment when Congress has already made a completed “violation of subsection (c)” an element of § 924(j). Under the ordinary public meaning of “in the course of a violation of,” § 924(j) necessarily subsumes § 924(c) on the same predicate and firearm use, so Blockburger treats § 924(c) as lesser-included and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement to permit two punishments for the same offense. Justice Barrett’s point that Congress knew how to draft explicit stacking provisions within § 924(c) underscores that we should not infer cumulative authorization from silence in § 924(j). Lora confirms § 924(j) is a distinct offense for sentencing mechanics, but it does not supply the clear textual authorization needed to impose duplicative § 924(c)+§ 924(j) convictions for the same conduct, so the redundant § 924(c) conviction must be vacated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a broad pro-cumulative-punishment policy, but as the Chief Justice Roberts explains, that language is most naturally read to ensure consecutiveness vis-à-vis the predicate “crime of violence/drug trafficking crime,” not to silently authorize a second conviction when Congress itself makes a completed § 924(c) violation an element of § 924(j). Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is necessarily lesser-included within § 924(j) on the same conduct, and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement to permit cumulative punishments; Justice Barrett’s point that Congress explicitly addressed stacking elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores the lack of that clear authorization here. Lora’s treatment of § 924(j) as distinct for sentencing mechanics further cuts against importing § 924(c)’s sentencing/stacking machinery by inference. Given the text and these precedents, the proper, narrow remedy is to vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving § 924(j) intact.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language signals a broad pro-stacking policy—still does not answer the narrower multiple-punishments question when § 924(c) is already an element of § 924(j). As Justice Kagan explains, Blockburger and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear indication that Congress authorized two convictions and sentences for the same § 924(c)-based conduct, and § 924(j)’s silence (against Congress’s demonstrated ability to specify stacking elsewhere) does not provide it. Lora, as the Chief Justice notes, reinforces that § 924(j) is not simply governed by § 924(c)’s sentencing commands, making it especially inappropriate to infer an unstated stacking rule that would predictably inflate sentences in already severe homicide cases. I therefore continue to think the proper remedy is to vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving the § 924(j) conviction intact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the broad “in addition to”/consecutive-sentencing language in § 924(c), but that text answers a different question: how a sentence imposed “under this subsection” relates to “any other term of imprisonment,” not whether Congress authorized an additional § 924(c) conviction when § 924(c) is already an element of § 924(j). As the Chief explains, Blockburger makes § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on the same predicate conduct, so Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement to permit cumulative punishments—and Justice Barrett’s point that Congress expressly provided stacking rules elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores that we do not have that clarity here. Lora, as several colleagues note, cuts against importing § 924(c)’s sentencing commands into § 924(j), making it even harder to infer an unstated cumulative-punishment authorization. The pragmatic, text-faithful remedy is to vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving § 924(j) intact.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the appeal to § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language as a broad stacking command, but that language is most naturally read—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain—to govern how a sentence imposed “under this subsection” relates to the predicate offense, not to authorize an extra § 924(c) conviction when Congress has already made a completed § 924(c) violation an element of § 924(j). Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is therefore a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on the same predicate conduct, and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement before we permit cumulative punishments for the same act—silence in § 924(j) does not qualify, especially given (as Justice Barrett notes) Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak expressly about stacking elsewhere in § 924(c). Lora, if anything, strengthens that conclusion by treating § 924(j) as a distinct offense with its own penalty scheme rather than a mandatory add-on, making it harder to infer an unstated cumulative-punishment authorization. I would vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction and leave the § 924(j) conviction undisturbed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language, but that reads as a general anti-concurrency rule for a sentence “under this subsection,” not as the kind of clear authorization Whalen/Garrett and Missouri v. Hunter require to impose a second conviction and punishment when § 924(c) is wholly embedded as an element of § 924(j). Chief Justice Roberts’s Blockburger analysis is persuasive: on the same predicate conduct, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), so we should not infer cumulative punishment from silence—especially where, as Justice Barrett notes, Congress elsewhere drafted explicit stacking provisions within § 924(c). Lora’s holding that § 924(j) is not subject to § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command further weakens the respondent’s inference that § 924(c)’s general consecutive directive silently carries over to authorize § 924(c)+§ 924(j) stacking for the same act. An institutionalist, narrow remedy—vacating the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving § 924(j) intact—fits precedent and avoids reading unstated penalties into the statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a broad stacking policy, but that text is most naturally limited to sentences imposed “under this subsection” and to ensuring § 924(c) runs consecutive to the predicate offense—not to authorizing an extra § 924(c) conviction when Congress has already made a completed § 924(c) violation an element of § 924(j). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, under Blockburger § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on the same predicate conduct, and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement to permit cumulative punishments for the same conduct; nothing in § 924(j) supplies it. Lora’s recognition (highlighted by Justice Kagan) that § 924(j) is not governed by § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive rule further undercuts the inference that Congress silently mandated stacking here. Given Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak expressly about stacking within § 924(c) (as Justice Alito notes), this silence leaves the presumption against multiple punishments unrebutted, so the redundant § 924(c) conviction should be vacated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language signals a broad pro-stacking policy, but as Chief Justice Roberts explains, those provisions most naturally ensure § 924(c) runs consecutive to the predicate crime—not that Congress silently authorized a second § 924(c) conviction when § 924(j) already incorporates a completed “violation of subsection (c).” Justice Kagan’s Blockburger framing is decisive for me: on the same predicate and firearm use, § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), so Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter demand a clear indication of cumulative intent, and § 924(j)’s silence (especially given Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak expressly about stacking within § 924(c)) does not meet that standard. Lora’s separation of § 924(j) from § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive-sentencing mechanics further undercuts importing § 924(c)’s general pro-consecutiveness into an unstated authorization for dual punishments. Given the practical consequences—routine overcharging and sentence inflation in already-severe homicide cases—I would vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction and leave the § 924(j) conviction intact.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 924(j) defines an offense that occurs only “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c), making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger and triggering the presumption against multiple punishments for the same conduct absent a clear indication of contrary congressional intent. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments only when the legislature has authorized them, but here neither § 924(j)’s text nor § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing provisions clearly speak to cumulating § 924(c) with § 924(j) for the same act, especially given Congress’s demonstrated ability to specify stacking elsewhere within § 924(c). Lora v. United States underscores that § 924(j) is a separate offense from § 924(c) for certain sentencing purposes, but it does not supply the necessary congressional authorization to impose two convictions and sentences for the same § 924(c)-based conduct. A narrow disposition vacating the § 924(c) conviction avoids a Double Jeopardy multiple-punishment problem while respecting Congress’s chosen penalties under § 924(j).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c), so a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation is necessarily an element of § 924(j), making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger v. United States. Under the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments doctrine, the dispositive question is whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishments for § 924(c) and § 924(j) based on the same conduct; the statutory text provides no such authorization, especially compared to § 924(c)’s explicit “in addition to”/consecutive-sentencing directives in other contexts. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative sentences when the legislature has made that intent clear, but here the incorporation of § 924(c) into § 924(j) coupled with Congress’s silence about stacking these two provisions leaves the Blockburger presumption unrebutted. Accordingly, one of the duplicative convictions (typically § 924(c)) must be vacated to avoid multiple punishment for the same offense.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes a violation of § 924(c) an element of the offense (death caused “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c)), so under Blockburger § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both charges rest on the same predicate crime and the same firearm use. In that setting, cumulative punishments are permissible only if Congress clearly indicated an intent to authorize them, and nothing in the text or structure of § 924(j) supplies such an indication—especially given that Congress elsewhere in § 924(c) spoke expressly when it wanted stacking and consecutive punishment. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments where the legislature has made that choice, but it does not dispense with the need to find that choice in the enacted law; here, the more natural reading is that § 924(j) provides an alternative, aggravated firearm-homicide offense rather than an automatic add-on to a separate § 924(c) conviction for the same conduct. Accordingly, imposing separate convictions and sentences for both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j) for the same act violates the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishment rule absent clearer congressional authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly requires that the killing occur “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c), so § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger’s elements test, triggering the presumption against multiple punishments for the same conduct. Nothing in the text or structure clearly rebuts that presumption: Congress included explicit cumulative-punishment and consecutive-sentencing directives in § 924(c) for other contexts, but it did not authorize stacking § 924(c) on top of § 924(j) for the same predicate offense. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments only when the legislature has clearly authorized them, and here that clear authorization is absent, so imposing convictions and sentences under both provisions would raise a serious Double Jeopardy multiple-punishment problem. Consistent with Lora’s careful attention to § 924(j)’s distinct design and sentencing consequences, one of the two convictions—typically the lesser § 924(c)—should be vacated to ensure fairness and prevent unnecessary overpunishment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element—death must be caused “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c)—so a § 924(c)(1)(A) offense is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States. In that circumstance, Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter permit cumulative punishments only if Congress has clearly indicated an intent to authorize them; § 924(c)’s general consecutive-sentencing rule does not speak to whether Congress meant a second, cumulative conviction when § 924(c) is already subsumed within § 924(j). The statutory structure reinforces the absence of such an indication: Congress expressly addressed stacking in parts of § 924(c) but did not do so for the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing, and after Lora v. United States confirms § 924(j) is not subject to § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive-sentencing command, it is hard to infer an unstated authorization for cumulative sentences here. Because there is no clear statutory signal rebutting the Blockburger presumption, one conviction (typically the lesser § 924(c)) must be vacated to avoid multiple punishment for the same offense under the Double Jeopardy Clause.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes a "violation of subsection (c)" an element, so every § 924(j) conviction necessarily includes all elements of § 924(c)(1)(A), rendering § 924(c) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger v. United States. In the multiple-punishments context, Blockburger operates as a rule of statutory construction: absent a clear indication Congress authorized cumulative punishment for the same conduct, courts presume Congress did not intend two punishments for the same offense. Nothing in § 924(j)'s text, or § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing language, clearly authorizes stacking a § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same predicate conduct, especially given Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak expressly about stacking within § 924(c). Under Missouri v. Hunter, the Double Jeopardy question turns on legislative intent, and here the best reading is that Congress did not authorize cumulative convictions and sentences.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element, so under Blockburger § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption that Congress did not intend cumulative punishments for the same conduct. Under Whalen and Garrett, that presumption yields only if there is a sufficiently clear indication of contrary congressional intent, but nothing in the text or structure of § 924(j) clearly authorizes stacking a separate § 924(c) conviction and sentence on top of § 924(j). Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments when the legislature clearly so provides, yet here the consecutive-sentencing language of § 924(c) and Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak explicitly when it wants stacking do not supply the needed clarity. Consistent with judicial restraint and practical workability, the proper remedy is to vacate the redundant § 924(c) conviction while leaving § 924(j) (and its sentencing range) in place.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(j) by its terms applies only when the defendant causes death “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c), making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States. In the multiple-punishments context, the Double Jeopardy inquiry turns on congressional intent, and Blockburger’s presumption against cumulative punishment yields only to a clear indication to the contrary. See Missouri v. Hunter and Garrett v. United States. Nothing in the text or structure of § 924(j), or in § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing provisions, clearly authorizes piling a § 924(c) conviction on top of a § 924(j) conviction for the same conduct—especially given Congress’s demonstrated ability to specify stacking rules expressly within § 924(c).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes a § 924(c) violation an element—death must occur “in the course of a violation of” § 924(c)—so under Blockburger the § 924(c)(1)(A) offense is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption that Congress did not authorize cumulative punishment for the same conduct. Nothing in § 924(j)’s text or placement within § 924 clearly rebuts that presumption, and Congress’s demonstrated practice of expressly authorizing stacking within § 924(c) underscores that silence here should not be read to permit dual convictions and sentences. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative punishments only where Congress has authorized them; absent a clear indication of such authorization, imposing both convictions for the same act risks unconstitutional multiple punishment under the Double Jeopardy Clause. Consistent with procedural fairness and avoiding unwarranted sentence inflation, the proper remedy is to vacate the lesser-included § 924(c) conviction.
